notes:
I found verse-by-verse comments on Isaiah 19 for every verse except v. 12, which none of the pages I read discussed directly. My sources were Enduring Word (David Guzik), Ellicott, Calvin, Matthew Henry, Gill, the Pulpit Commentary, Spurgeon, Ligonier and a few others quoted on biblehub and studylight. I ran out of searches before reaching the Lutheran, Methodist, Catholic, Orthodox, netbible.org or bibleodyssey.org pages. Those gaps are listed at the end.

## Verse-by-verse notes

**v. 1**
- Guzik says God made Egypt's idols "totter" at the Exodus, aiming each plague at a particular Egyptian god, and Isaiah says He will do it again. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-19/
- Ellicott: the long-delayed judgment is finally coming, swift as a cloud driven by the storm-wind, upon the idols of Egypt. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/19.htm
- On the same page, Poole notes that clouds are rare in Egypt, so the appearance of a cloud was a kind of prodigy, and a prognostic of some grievous calamity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/19-1.htm
- Calvin: the idols will be no help to the Egyptians, even though they trust them for protection. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/19-1.html
- **A disputed reading.** Gill reports that Jerome and others connected this verse to the infant Christ's flight into Egypt. Salmeron passed on a story that when Christ entered Heliopolis, all the idols in its temple fell. Gill calls this a weak application. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nlv/isaiah/19-1.html
  - Calvin also rejects it: he pass[es] by the foolish notion which many have entertained, as to the idols which Christ overthrew in Egypt. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/isaiah-19.html
  - Trapp mentions the same story and thinks the verse only means Egypt's gods would be discredited. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/trapp_john/isa-19.cfm
  - Guzik, by contrast, quotes Athanasius (a 4th-century church father) seeing the verse fulfilled when the Lord, "riding as on a cloud," came down in the body and ended idol worship in Egypt. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-19/

**v. 2**
- Guzik: this predicts civil war, which was indirectly God's judgment. He quotes Poole, who says Egypt was later split into twelve warring kingdoms. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-19/
- Ellicott ties the strife to the fall of Ethiopian rule over Egypt (Sargon, 720 BC). He also cites Herodotus on Egypt breaking up into twelve kingdoms. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/19.htm

**v. 3**
- Guzik: when God judges a nation, He often seems to remove sound advice from its leaders, and they turn to idols and mediums instead. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-19/
- Ellicott: Egypt had long been known for magic (Exodus 7–8). In a panic, when ordinary statesmen fail, people turn to oracles and fortune-telling. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/19.htm

**v. 4**
- Guzik: God judges a nation's leadership in two ways, by taking away competent leaders and by giving it cruel rulers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-19/
- Ellicott: so many oppressors followed in Egypt's history that it is hard to choose one. Sargon, Esarhaddon, Psammetichus, Nebuchadnezzar and Cambyses have all been proposed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/19.htm
- Calvin points out that "cruel" is singular but "lords" is plural, which is harder to bear than one master. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/isaiah-19.html

**vv. 5–7**
- Guzik: the Nile was the key to Egypt's farming and economy, so drying it up would wreck the nation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-19/
- Ellicott:
  - The "sea" in older translations means the Nile.
  - The disaster comes partly from failed yearly floods and partly from irrigation being neglected during the civil war.
  - The "brooks" are the channels of the Delta.
  - The Nile valley would become as barren as the desert on either side.
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/19.htm

**vv. 8–10**
- Ellicott:
  - Fish was a staple food for ordinary Egyptians.
  - Fine flax was used for priests' clothing and for wrapping mummies.
  - "Pillars" in v. 10 means the props of the state, and "those who work for wages" means ordinary people.
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/19.htm
- Guzik: the ecological disaster makes the workers cry out. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-19/

**v. 11**
- Ellicott: Zoan (Greek Tanis) was a major Delta city and once Rameses II's capital. Its princes were probably priest-magicians who boasted of their wisdom and ancestry. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/19.htm

**v. 12**
- Not covered directly in my sources. The nearest comments: Guzik (on vv. 11–15) says true wisdom means knowing what the LORD of hosts has planned, not just facts and strategies. Ellicott (on v. 11) asks whether Egypt's counsellors can reveal the future as the prophet can. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-19/ and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/19.htm

**vv. 13–15**
- Ellicott:
  - Noph is Memphis.
  - The "cornerstones" are the priest-rulers who claimed top rank among Egypt's classes.
  - In v. 14 God pours out a "spirit of giddiness." Like 1 Kings 22:22, this is judicial blindness, meaning God sending confusion as a judgment.
  - "Head or tail, palm or reed" (v. 15) stands for every class of people (see Isaiah 9:14).
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/19.htm

**v. 16**
- Guzik: all God needs to do is wave His hand, and Egypt is terrified. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-19/
- Ellicott: comparing a nation to women was a common image of panic in ancient poetry. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/19.htm

**v. 17**
- Guzik: this is a dramatic reversal, because Judah had long lived in Egypt's shadow. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-19/
- The Pulpit Commentary reads it historically. Egypt dreaded Judah as the place Assyrian armies seemed to march from, and The fear felt by the Egyptians was not a religious fear. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/19.htm

**v. 18**
- Ligonier: "language of Canaan" means Hebrew. It is a picture of Egypt becoming Israel's ally and taking up Israel's faith. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/egypt-redeemed
- Ellicott: the "five cities" are either a round number or Egypt's chief cities. The oath is an oath of loyalty, a kind of covenant of obedience. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/19.htm
- Matthew Henry: Converting grace, by changing the heart, changes the language. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/isaiah/19.htm
- Barnes treats "five" as an unspecified number. JFB (Jamieson-Fausset-Brown) lists possible cities such as Heliopolis, Migdol, Tahpanhes and Memphis. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/19-18.htm
- **City of the Sun or City of Destruction?** The Hebrew wording is disputed.
  - Ellicott sees a pun on On/Heliopolis (City of the Sun) that predicts the sun-idols will be destroyed.
  - The Latin Vulgate has "city of the sun"; the Greek Septuagint has "city of righteousness."
  - Ellicott links the Septuagint reading to the Jewish temple Onias IV built at Leontopolis.
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/19.htm
- Guzik prefers "City of the Sun," meaning Heliopolis. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-19/

**v. 19**
- Calvin: the altar stands for the pure worship of God, and this speaks of Christ's kingdom. Onias wickedly twisted the verse to justify his temple. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/isaiah-19.html
- Ellicott: like the Jordan tribes' altar in Joshua 22, it is an altar of "witness," not a rival worship centre. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/19-19.htm
- Poole: not a Levitical, but a spiritual and evangelical altar. The prophets often describe gospel worship in the language of the Law. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/19-19.htm
- Gill: the altar is Christ Himself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/19-19.htm
- JFB: the altar is a memorial, not for sacrifice, and the pillar on the border proclaims a shared faith to Egypt and Judah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/19-19.htm
- Keil and Delitzsch: the Onias temple can't be the fulfilment, because Jews built it for Jews. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/19-19.htm
- Another commentator on that page (not named in the excerpt) says the altar was meant for real sacrifices and so went beyond the Mosaic one-altar law. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/19-19.htm
- Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) reads it as a future time when Egypt becomes a centre for worshipping the Lord. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/19-19.html

**v. 20**
- **Who is the "savior"?** This is the main point of disagreement.
  - **Christ:** Calvin says it can mean no other than Christ. Gill, Matthew Henry and the Geneva Study Bible agree. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/19-20.html and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/19-20.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary sees no earthly deliverer, but the Saviour from sin and Satan. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/19-20.htm
  - **Alexander the Great or the Ptolemies:** Barnes thinks Alexander more likely (following Vitringa and Newton) and says the Christ reading doesn't fit the context. JFB also leans to Alexander. Grotius suggested the angel who destroyed Sennacherib's army. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/19-20.html and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/19-20.htm
  - **Both:** Ellicott sees deliverers like Israel's judges, with a "higher fulfilment" in the gospel reaching Egypt. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/19-20.htm
  - Bob Utley (bible.org) says it first means someone who defeats the cruel master of v. 4, but ultimately points to the Messiah. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-19
- Spurgeon (Baptist) preached on this verse: a great sinner needs a great Saviour. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/19-20.html

**v. 21**
- Pulpit: "shall be known" is better "shall make himself known," through answered prayer and the Spirit's work. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/19-21.htm
- Pulpit also says Christian Egypt offered sacrifice in the same sense as the rest of the Church (Malachi 1:11). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/19.htm
- Guzik says this has been fulfilled in history (a million Jews in Egypt in Jesus' day, then a strong church for centuries). But he expects the altar and sacrifices most likely in the Millennium, as a memorial of Christ's work, never as atonement. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-19/
- Calvin: vows must be governed by God's word, not by what we please. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/isaiah-19.html

**v. 22**
- Calvin's order: suffering prepares people to repent, then come healing, pardon, reconciliation and an end to punishment. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/isaiah-19.html
- Guzik: whatever judgment God allows, His aim is repentance and healing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-19/

**v. 23**
- Pulpit: the wording echoes Isaiah 11:16, but the purpose differs. There the highway brought Israel home; here it gives the three peoples free contact. "Serve" here means "worship." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/19.htm
- One biblehub article links the highway to the "highway of holiness" (35:8) and to a future millennial peace. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_are_Egypt_Assyria_blessed_in_Isaiah_19_25.htm

**vv. 24–25**
- Ellicott: Assyria is God's instrument, but Israel has the proud pre-eminence of being His "inheritance." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/19.htm
- Pulpit:
  - "Him" means a threefold Israel spread across the three lands.
  - The three countries can bless the world because God's blessing rests on them.
  - It links this to Christianity's later spread in Syria, Mesopotamia and Persia.
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/19.htm
- Guzik: calling Egypt "My people" is remarkable, and saying it of hated Assyria is almost unbelievable. He applies "inheritance" to believers (Ephesians 1:18). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-19/
- One biblehub article sees the promise to Abraham (Genesis 12:3) being fulfilled here. It says Gentiles are grafted in without cancelling Israel's election. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_are_Egypt_Assyria_blessed_in_Isaiah_19_25.htm
- Spurgeon treats the promise as still to be fulfilled and as encouragement for missions. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/19-19.html

## Where the traditions really differ
- **vv. 19–21, altar and sacrifices:**
  - Reformed and Puritan writers read them as symbols of gospel worship: Calvin, Poole and Matthew Henry. Gill, a Baptist, goes further and makes the altar Christ.
  - Calvary Chapel teachers expect a literal future. Guzik foresees memorial sacrifices in the Millennium; Smith sees Egypt becoming a centre of worship.
  - Calvin, Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch all deny that Onias's temple was the fulfilment.
  - URLs: see vv. 19 and 21 above.
- **v. 20, the savior:**
  - Christ: Calvin, Gill, Matthew Henry, the Geneva Study Bible and the Pulpit Commentary.
  - A historical ruler such as Alexander: Barnes and JFB.
  - Both, a near and a far meaning: Ellicott and Utley.
  - URLs: see v. 20 above.

## Other views
- **The early Church:** Jerome's flight-into-Egypt reading of v. 1 (reported by Gill) and Athanasius's view that Christ's coming fulfilled vv. 1 and 21 (quoted by Guzik). See v. 1.
- **Ancient translations:** the Septuagint has "city of righteousness" and the Vulgate "city of the sun" in v. 18. In v. 20 the Septuagint reads the "great one" as "judging, he shall save." See vv. 18 and 20.
